paper.title: Extensive green roofs and indoor overheating in top-floor social-housing flats: a paired field study

paper_doc.running_head: ARTICLE IN PRESS · J. Fake Building Physics (2025) 104127 · doi:10.9999/fake.2025.027
paper_doc.title: Extensive green roofs and indoor overheating in top-floor social-housing flats: a paired field study
paper_doc.authors: Nkechi Okafor, Elin Lindqvist, Paolo Marchetti · Department of Building Physics, Fake Institute of Technology
paper_doc.abstract: Top-floor flats in post-war social housing overheat during heatwaves, and extensive green roofs are often proposed as a passive retrofit that landlords can install without decanting tenants. Field evidence for their effect on indoor conditions, as opposed to roof-surface temperatures, is thin. We monitored 24 pairs of top-floor flats in six matched blocks, one block of each pair retrofitted with an extensive sedum roof, through two summers. Indoor air temperature and relative humidity were logged every ten minutes in the living room and main bedroom, roof-surface temperature was logged on both roof types, and occupants kept weekly diaries of window opening, fan use and time spent at home. We compare daily peak indoor temperatures and the hours spent above common overheating thresholds between the paired flats, adjusting for orientation, occupancy and window opening, and we report how the difference varied with outdoor conditions. We close by discussing what the measured differences mean for retrofit programmes and for the city-scale heat models that rely on them.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Heatwaves are becoming longer and more frequent in mid-latitude cities, and the health burden they carry falls unevenly. Older residents, people with chronic illness and people living alone are most at risk, and they are over-represented in social housing. Within a block, the top floor is the warmest place to live: the roof absorbs solar radiation all day and releases heat into the flats below well into the night, when occupants most need their homes to cool down. Night-time indoor temperature, more than daytime peaks, is linked to poor sleep and to excess deaths during heat events.
Retrofit options for the top floor fall into three groups. Reflective coatings reduce the solar gain of the roof surface; added insulation slows the flow of heat through the roof deck; and vegetated roofs combine shading, evapotranspiration and added thermal mass. Extensive green roofs, with a thin substrate and drought-tolerant plants such as sedum, are light enough to be installed on many existing flat roofs without structural work, and they bring other benefits that landlords and city authorities value: stormwater retention, habitat for pollinators and a longer life for the waterproofing membrane beneath them.
The evidence on cooling is uneven. Laboratory and test-cell studies consistently show large reductions in roof-surface temperature, often of 20 °C or more on clear afternoons. Far fewer studies have measured what happens indoors, in occupied homes, where the roof is only one of several paths for heat and where occupants open windows, draw curtains and run fans. Simulation studies fill the gap with assumed values, and the values they assume vary by a factor of several. City-scale estimates of avoided heat exposure, which inform public funding for retrofit, are only as good as these assumptions.
We set out to measure the indoor effect directly. The study had three aims: to estimate the difference in daily peak indoor temperature between otherwise similar top-floor flats with and without an extensive green roof during heatwaves; to estimate the difference in time spent above common overheating thresholds; and to examine how these differences depend on outdoor conditions and on occupant behaviour.

sections.heading: 2. Study blocks and retrofit
sections.text:
The study took place in a social-housing estate built between 1962 and 1968, managed by a single housing association. The estate consists of four- and five-storey blocks of identical design: load-bearing brick cross-walls, precast concrete floor and roof slabs, and a flat roof finished with bituminous felt over 50 mm of mineral-wool insulation added in the 1990s. Flats are two-bedroom, with the living room and main bedroom on the same side of the block.
In 2022 the housing association retrofitted the roofs of three blocks with an extensive green roof as part of a waterproofing renewal. The build-up comprised a root-resistant membrane, a drainage and water-retention mat, 80 mm of lightweight mineral substrate and a pre-grown sedum blanket. No irrigation was installed. The other blocks on the estate received a like-for-like felt renewal at the same time, which gave us a set of control roofs of the same age and insulation level.
We paired each retrofitted block with a control block of the same storey count and orientation, chosen before any indoor data were collected. Within each pair we recruited four top-floor flats per block, matching flats by position in the block (end or middle) wherever households agreed to take part. Of the 61 top-floor households approached, 48 agreed. Table 1 summarises the blocks.

table.caption: Table 1. Characteristics of the paired blocks.

sections.heading: 3. Monitoring and data processing
sections.text:
Each flat was fitted with two temperature and humidity loggers, one in the living room and one in the main bedroom, mounted on an internal wall at 1.1 m above the floor and away from radiators, windows and direct sunlight. The loggers have a stated accuracy of ±0.2 °C and recorded every ten minutes. On each roof, two surface sensors were installed: on the green roofs beneath the sedum blanket at the substrate surface, and on the control roofs directly on the felt. A weather station on the roof of a neighbouring block recorded outdoor air temperature, global solar radiation, wind speed and rainfall.
Monitoring ran from 1 June to 15 September in 2023 and in 2024. Households were visited at the start and end of each summer to check loggers and download data, and once in the middle of each summer to replace batteries. Each week, households completed a short diary: which windows they had opened during the day and at night, whether they had used an electric fan, and on how many days someone had been at home for most of the afternoon. Diary completion was high, with 91% of household-weeks returned.
We defined heatwave days as days within a run of at least three consecutive days on which the outdoor maximum reached 27 °C or more, which follows the threshold used by the national weather service for the region. The daily peak indoor temperature was the highest ten-minute reading in the living room between 06:00 and 24:00. Hours above thresholds were counted from the ten-minute series, using 26 °C for bedrooms at night and 28 °C for living rooms during the day, in line with common overheating criteria for dwellings.
Gaps of up to one hour were filled by linear interpolation; longer gaps were left missing. Readings outside the logger's operating range or showing a step change at a site visit were flagged and checked against the diary and the paired flat. In total, 2.7% of ten-minute readings were missing or removed.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Plan of a typical top-floor flat and section through the roof build-ups, showing the positions of the living-room and bedroom loggers and of the roof-surface sensors on the green and control roofs.

sections.heading: 4. Statistical analysis
sections.text:
The unit of analysis was the flat-day. For each heatwave day, we modelled the daily peak indoor temperature with a linear mixed model that included roof type as a fixed effect, together with the outdoor maximum temperature, the daily total of global solar radiation, the position of the flat in the block, the number of occupants, and diary indicators for daytime window opening and fan use. Random intercepts for block pair, flat and day accounted for the matched design and for repeated measures. Hours above threshold were modelled with a negative binomial mixed model with the same structure.
To examine how the effect of the green roof varied with outdoor conditions, we added an interaction between roof type and outdoor maximum temperature. We checked the robustness of the main estimate by refitting the model without diary variables, by excluding the pair with the largest difference in household size, and by restricting the analysis to the hottest heatwave of each summer. The analysis plan was written before the 2024 monitoring season, and the 2024 data were analysed with the code developed on the 2023 data. Analyses were run in R with the lme4 and glmmTMB packages.

sections.heading: 5.1 Weather during the monitoring periods
sections.text: Both summers were warmer than the 1991–2020 average for the region. Three heatwaves met our definition: one in July 2023 and two in 2024, one in late June and one in August. Together they gave 19 heatwave days, summarised in Table 2. Rain fell on two of the heatwave days, both in the June 2024 event, and wind speeds were low throughout. The sedum blanket remained in good condition through both summers, although it browned visibly during the August 2024 event, when the substrate had been dry for more than two weeks.

table.caption: Table 2. Heatwaves during the monitoring periods.

sections.heading: 5.2 Peak indoor temperatures
sections.text:
During the three heatwave periods, the mean daily peak indoor temperature in green-roofed flats was 2.1 °C lower than in the paired control flats (95% CI 1.6 to 2.6 °C), after adjustment for outdoor conditions, flat position, occupancy and occupant behaviour. The difference was present in every block pair and in each of the three heatwaves. It was larger on the hottest days: the interaction with outdoor maximum temperature indicated that the gap widened as outdoor conditions became more extreme, and the gap was smallest during the June 2024 event, which included the two rainy days.
Green-roofed flats also spent less time above the overheating thresholds. Across heatwave days, living rooms in green-roofed flats spent 41% fewer hours above 28 °C than those in control flats, and bedrooms showed a similar pattern for night-time hours above 26 °C. Figure 2 shows the daily course of living-room temperature on a typical heatwave day for one block pair.

figure.caption: Figure 2. Living-room air temperature over 24 hours on a heatwave day, for the four green-roofed and four control flats of one block pair, with outdoor air temperature for reference.

sections.heading: 5.3 Roof surfaces, occupant behaviour and sensitivity checks
sections.text:
Roof-surface temperatures followed the pattern reported in test-cell studies: on clear heatwave afternoons the felt of the control roofs was far hotter than the substrate surface beneath the sedum, and the green roofs stayed cooler through the evening. The difference shrank after the August 2024 dry spell, when the browned sedum gave less shade and the dry substrate held less water.
Occupant behaviour was similar in the two groups. Households in both groups opened windows at night on most heatwave nights and used fans on about half of the heatwave days. The time spent at home in the afternoon did not differ between groups. Because occupants in hot flats might open windows more, behaviour could in principle mediate part of the roof effect; including or excluding the diary variables changed the main estimate only slightly.
The sensitivity checks gave estimates close to the main result. Excluding the pair with the largest difference in household size, and restricting the analysis to the hottest heatwave of each summer, both left the direction and approximate size of the difference unchanged.

sections.heading: 6. Discussion
sections.text:
In occupied top-floor flats, an extensive green roof installed during a routine waterproofing renewal was associated with lower peak indoor temperatures and with fewer hours above overheating thresholds during heatwaves. The matched design, with paired blocks of the same age, construction and insulation, and the adjustment for occupant behaviour make it unlikely that the difference reflects differences between households rather than between roofs.
The indoor effect we measured is much smaller than the reductions in roof-surface temperature that dominate the literature, and it should be. The roof is one of several paths for heat into a top-floor flat; walls, windows and ventilation air all contribute, and the existing insulation already damps the flow of heat through the roof deck. Studies that infer indoor benefits from roof-surface measurements, or that model the roof alone, are likely to overstate what occupants will experience.
The widening of the gap on the hottest days matters for health. It is on these days that indoor temperatures in top-floor flats move into the range associated with harm, and it is then that a passive measure that needs no energy and no action by occupants is most valuable. The smaller gap after the dry spell in August 2024 points the other way: without irrigation, an extensive roof gives less cooling when it has been dry for some time, which is common late in a hot summer. Landlords weighing a green roof against a reflective coating or added insulation should consider the local rainfall pattern, and the option of irrigation where water is available.
Our results bear on the city-scale models used to estimate the benefit of retrofit programmes. Such models need a value for the indoor cooling effect of each measure, and measured values from occupied dwellings are rare. We hope the estimate reported here, together with its uncertainty, will be of use to modellers, provided its conditions are kept in mind: an existing insulated concrete roof, an unirrigated sedum system and a temperate climate with occasional heatwaves.

figure.caption: Figure 3. Estimated difference in daily peak indoor temperature between green-roofed and control flats as a function of the outdoor maximum temperature, from the model with an interaction term, with its 95% confidence band.

sections.heading: 7. Limitations
sections.text: The study has several limitations. The number of blocks is small, and the retrofit was not randomised: the housing association chose which blocks received green roofs, partly on structural grounds. We matched pairs before collecting indoor data and adjusted for measured differences, but unmeasured differences between blocks may remain. Only top-floor flats were monitored, so we cannot say how far the effect reaches into the floors below. The study covered two summers in one climate; the effect in hotter or drier climates, or with deeper substrates, may differ. Diary data are self-reported and coarse, and they cannot capture how long windows were open or how far. Finally, the loggers measured air temperature only, while thermal comfort also depends on radiant temperature, humidity and air movement.

sections.heading: 8. Conclusions
sections.text: Extensive green roofs fitted to existing insulated flat roofs reduced peak indoor temperatures and overheating hours in the top-floor flats below during heatwaves, with the largest benefit on the hottest days and a smaller one after long dry spells. The indoor effect is far smaller than the effect on roof-surface temperature, and models of retrofit benefit should use indoor measurements rather than surface ones. Green roofs are a reasonable component of a heat-resilience retrofit for top-floor flats, alongside measures that address windows, shading and night-time ventilation.

sections.heading: Acknowledgements and data availability
sections.text: We thank the residents who took part and the housing association's asset management team for access to the blocks and their retrofit records. The study received no external funding. The authors declare no competing interests. Anonymised ten-minute data and the analysis code are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.

documents.title: WITHDRAWN: Extensive green roofs and indoor overheating in top-floor social-housing flats: a paired field study
documents.text:
WITHDRAWN: Extensive green roofs and indoor overheating in top-floor social-housing flats: a paired field study

This article has been withdrawn at the request of the editor. After the article was accepted, the editor was informed that the indoor temperature records analysed in it had been processed with an incorrect sensor calibration, so the reported results cannot be relied on. The article was withdrawn before final publication, and its full text and PDF have been replaced by this statement. The Publisher apologizes for any inconvenience this may cause.

draft_doc.title: Avoided heat exposure from green-roof retrofits of social housing: a city-scale estimate
draft_doc.authors: Wei Tan, Sadia Rahman · School of Urban Health, Fake University
draft_doc.abstract: Cities are funding passive retrofits of social housing to protect vulnerable residents from heat, but the benefit of each measure is rarely estimated at the scale at which decisions are made. We combine a stock model of the city's social-housing blocks with a simple indoor heat model and thirty years of local weather records to estimate how many person-hours of exposure to indoor overheating a programme of extensive green-roof retrofits would avoid among residents of top-floor flats. We describe the stock model, the indoor heat model and its parameters, and the exposure metric, and we compare the estimated benefit with that of reflective roof coatings and of roof insulation upgrades. We discuss what the estimate means for the city's retrofit programme and where it is most uncertain.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Exposure to high indoor temperatures during heatwaves harms health, and the harm is concentrated among older residents, people with chronic illness and people who live alone [1, 2]. Night-time indoor temperature is particularly important, because bodies that cannot cool overnight carry the strain into the next day [3]. In many cities these groups are over-represented in social housing, and within a block the top floor is the warmest place to live, because the roof gains heat all day and releases it into the flats below in the evening and at night [4, 5].
Passive retrofits are attractive for this stock because they need no energy and no action by residents. The options for the roof are well known: reflective coatings, added insulation and vegetated roofs [6–8]. Each has costs and co-benefits beyond cooling. Extensive green roofs retain stormwater, support pollinators and extend the life of the waterproofing beneath them [9, 10], and they can often be installed on existing flat roofs during routine waterproofing renewals. Reflective coatings are cheap but lose reflectance as they weather [11]. Insulation upgrades help in winter as well as summer but are disruptive when the roof deck must be opened [12].
Public retrofit programmes must choose between these options across thousands of blocks. City-scale estimates of avoided heat exposure are one input to that choice [13], and several have been published for other cities, using a range of building models and exposure metrics [15–17]. Most rely on simulation of representative dwellings, with the effect of each measure set from the literature. The values used for green roofs vary widely between studies [18], partly because much of the evidence concerns roof-surface temperatures rather than indoor conditions [19, 20], and the effect on the roof surface is many times larger than the effect indoors.
Our city is about to commit funding for a ten-year programme of roof works on its social-housing stock, and the programme board asked for an estimate of the heat-exposure benefit of including green roofs where structurally possible. This paper reports that estimate. We aimed to keep the model simple enough to be understood and checked by the programme board, and to base its key parameter on measurements in occupied dwellings rather than on simulation or surface data.

sections.heading: 2.1 Housing stock
sections.text: The city's social-housing register lists 1,412 blocks with flat roofs, of which 1,036 are of the post-war concrete-slab type for which green-roof retrofits are structurally feasible without strengthening, according to the landlords' condition surveys. For each block, the register gives the number of storeys, the number of flats on the top floor, the roof area and the date of the last waterproofing renewal. We linked the register to the city's tenancy records, which give household size and the age of the oldest resident, so that exposure can be counted for all residents and for residents aged 75 and over separately. Table 1 summarises the stock.

table.caption: Table 1. Flat-roofed social-housing blocks in the city.

sections.heading: 2.2 Indoor heat model and parameters
sections.text:
We estimate the hourly living-room temperature of a top-floor flat from the outdoor temperature with a lumped-parameter model fitted to monitoring data from a sample of the city's top-floor flats [21]. The model has a thermal time constant, a gain for solar radiation and an offset for internal gains, and it reproduces the daily peak indoor temperature of the monitored flats to within half a degree on most days. Each retrofit enters the model as a reduction in the daily peak indoor temperature, spread over the day in proportion to the solar gain.
We set the indoor cooling effect of a green roof in the model to 2.1 °C, the reduction in daily peak indoor temperature measured during heatwaves in the paired field study of top-floor social-housing flats by Okafor et al. [14]. We chose this study because it measured indoor temperature in occupied flats of the same construction type as most of our stock, with a matched design and adjustment for occupant behaviour. For reflective coatings and for insulation upgrades we used the values from the comparison by Hughes and Mori [22], which was based on simulation calibrated against monitored dwellings.
We ran the model with hourly weather records for 1994–2023 from the city's main weather station [23], and with the same records shifted by the regional warming projected for the 2040s [24].

figure.caption: Figure 1. Structure of the estimate: housing stock, indoor heat model with a retrofit parameter for each measure, hourly weather, and the exposure metric.

sections.heading: 2.3 Exposure metric
sections.text: We count person-hours of exposure to indoor overheating as the number of hours in which the modelled living-room temperature exceeds 28 °C between 06:00 and 24:00, multiplied by the number of residents of the flat. This follows the overheating criterion for living rooms used in national guidance for dwellings [16]. We report the annual average over the weather record, for all residents and for residents aged 75 and over, and the share of person-hours avoided by each retrofit compared with no retrofit.

sections.heading: 3. Results
sections.text:
Without any retrofit, residents of top-floor flats in post-war concrete-slab blocks are exposed to an estimated annual average of 1.9 million person-hours of living-room temperatures above 28 °C under current weather, and to about twice that under the weather projected for the 2040s. Residents aged 75 and over account for about a fifth of the total.
With the green-roof parameter described in Section 2.2, retrofitting all structurally feasible blocks avoids about half of these person-hours under current weather, and a somewhat smaller share under the 2040s weather, because more of the remaining hours occur in long heatwaves when indoor temperatures stay high even with the retrofit. Reflective coatings avoid a smaller share, and insulation upgrades a smaller share still. Figure 2 shows the avoided person-hours by measure and weather scenario.

figure.caption: Figure 2. Annual person-hours above 28 °C in top-floor living rooms, without retrofit and with each roof measure, under current and 2040s weather.

sections.heading: 4. Discussion
sections.text:
Our estimate suggests that green roofs, installed during the waterproofing renewals the city is planning anyway, would avoid a large share of the indoor heat exposure of top-floor residents in the city's post-war blocks. The estimate rests above all on the size of the indoor cooling effect: the stock and weather inputs are well documented, and the exposure metric is standard, but the green-roof result scales almost directly with the 2.1 °C reduction in peak indoor temperature that we take from Okafor et al. [14]. If that value were halved, the share of avoided person-hours would fall by roughly the same proportion, and green roofs would no longer outperform reflective coatings.
This dependence is why we based the parameter on measurements in occupied flats rather than on the surface temperature reductions common in the literature [19, 20]. Using surface data would have produced an estimate several times larger and, in our view, misleading.
The estimate has other limitations. The lumped-parameter model treats every top-floor flat of a block type as alike, ignoring orientation and position in the block. It models living rooms only, while night-time bedroom temperatures matter for health [3]. And it ignores the loss of cooling from unirrigated green roofs during long dry spells, which could reduce the benefit late in hot summers [25].
For the programme board, the main conclusion is that green roofs merit inclusion in the roof-works programme where they are structurally feasible, and that the decision should be revisited if better measurements of the indoor effect become available.

sections.heading: 5. Conclusions
sections.text: A simple city-scale model, with its key parameter taken from field measurements in occupied flats, suggests that green-roof retrofits of the city's post-war social-housing blocks would substantially reduce indoor heat exposure among top-floor residents. The result depends strongly on the indoor cooling effect assumed for green roofs.

expected.why: RE-changes-explained.md §1–4, Other: withdrawal (and §8 Other Crossref types, self-referencing withdrawal; §5.3: for a withdrawal the content is gone, and only the notice and the stored PDF remain). The withdrawal is self-referencing, so the alert's notice DOI is the paper's own and the pipeline stores no notice document, only the current copy, whose title now starts "WITHDRAWN:" and whose text and PDF are the statement "This article has been withdrawn at the request of the editor", giving the reason "the reported results cannot be relied on". The current copy shows a change, so this isn't R3's 'own DOI, nothing changed' (about_this_paper yes, not no). Rubric: a withdrawal of the content is high, even though the rule's alert_severity for other is medium. The draft's Methods sets its model parameter to "2.1 °C" from the paper (methods_or_data), and its Discussion says its result rests on it (key_evidence): high x either = high. Only the stored PDF still holds the findings, and it predates the withdrawal.
